newsitem.title: UK: London gold fixes down as dealers ponder central bank sales.
newsitem.headline: London gold fixes down as dealers ponder central bank sales.

text.p: Gold fixed at a fresh low on Friday since April 25, 1994, the nadir hit the previous morning, after coming under pressure early, dealers said.
Some dealers also said the steady and high volume selling of the past few weeks had the stamp of a central bank.
Fear that a central bank could begin to sell from its gold reserves has kept the market cowed for weeks.
Gold was fixed at $371.90 per ounce down from the $372.65 on Thursday afternoon when it closed at $372.45/$372.95.
Selling into the Hong Kong and Tokyo markets by Australian producers, investment funds and out of Europe was cited as moving the gold price lower in the Far East.
"Selling has been steady and the bearish sentiment overwhelming," one dealer said.
"We are so close to a round number ($370.00) that this is inevitably going to be suggested as a target," he added.
However the feeling was that the professionals in Europe would square their books by midday and gold would drift out of the week at slightly higher than its morning levels.

Concerted selling in high volume has taken the spot price down from around $384.00 in late October while pumping short term lease (borrowing) rates up from under 1.70 percent for a month to over 3.00 percent earlier this week.

"It is very reminiscent of the last time the Dutch central bank sold a lot of gold (in late 1992 early 1993)," one dealer said. "It looks highly likely that a central bank has been involved," he added.
Along with other dealers he argued that the volume of selling plus the impact on lease rates was beyond the capacity of investment funds selling the market short.
"Producers have obviously been selling as well because if they are under hedged, there are going to be levels at which they panic," one dealer said.
Platinum was also weaker on Thursday morning, down $1.00 on its close at $374.25/$375.25. It fixed at its lowest level since December 6, 1993 on Thursday.
"Demand usually picks up at this time of year but it hasn't, inventories are high, the funds are short and going shorter and available material cannot be absorbed," one dealer explained.
He added that Russia has not been an active open market seller "for about six months".
New pressure could come on platinum as its premium over gold narrows encouraging spread trading, he added. Palladium and silver were unchanged at $114/$115 and $4.73/$4.75.
